questions.stem: A 67 year old man has a PSA test at a health check. He has no urinary symptoms, weight loss or bone pain. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg. Digital rectal examination shows a firm, irregular, asymmetric prostate with loss of the central sulcus. His PSA is shown (see item resources).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A markedly raised PSA with a firm, irregular, asymmetric prostate and loss of the sulcus is prostate cancer; it often has no urinary symptoms because it arises peripherally.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
An abnormal DRE and a high PSA without LUTS.

elim: Causes fever, perineal pain and an exquisitely tender gland.
Gives a smooth, symmetrical gland and a normal or mildly raised PSA, usually with LUTS.
Presents with painless haematuria and does not change the prostate on DRE.
Causes fever and a fluctuant, tender prostate.

steps.x: D. Prostate cancer. Irregular asymmetric gland + high PSA = prostate cancer.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has a PSA of 19 µg/L (<4) and a hard nodule in the right lobe of the prostate. MRI shows a PI-RADS 5 lesion. Transperineal biopsies are taken and show malignant glands infiltrating the stroma.
questions.q: Which is the most likely histological type of tumour?
questions.e: Prostate cancer is usually an adenocarcinoma of the glandular epithelium, and it is the most common cancer in men in the UK.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely histological type of tumour? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Malignant glands.

elim: Rare in the prostate and not glandular.
A rare, aggressive neuroendocrine prostate tumour.
Rare in the prostate.
A bladder and urothelial tumour, not the usual prostatic type.

steps.x: A. Adenocarcinoma. Prostate cancer = adenocarcinoma.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man has a PSA of 9 µg/L (<4). He has no urinary symptoms. Digital rectal examination reveals a hard nodule on the posterior aspect of the left lobe. Biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma.
questions.q: Which zone of the prostate is the tumour most likely to have arisen in?
questions.e: More than 75% of prostate adenocarcinomas arise in the peripheral zone, at the posterior aspect, which is why they are palpable on DRE.

steps.x: The question asks: Which zone of the prostate is the tumour most likely to have arisen in? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: hard nodule on the posterior aspect
steps.x: A posterior, palpable tumour without obstruction.

elim: Non-glandular and rarely the site of cancer.
Only about 5% of prostate cancers arise here.
Not part of the prostate.
The site of BPH, not most cancers.

steps.x: C. Peripheral zone. Cancer = peripheral zone (>75%); BPH = transition zone.

questions.stem: A 52 year old Black Caribbean man asks his GP about prostate cancer screening. He does not smoke, drinks 6 units a week and had a vasectomy 15 years ago. He has mild nocturia. His BMI is 26 kg/m².
questions.q: Which is the most important risk factor for prostate cancer in his history?
questions.e: Afro-Caribbean ethnicity is a major risk factor for prostate cancer, alongside BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most important risk factor for prostate cancer in his history? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Ethnicity.

elim: His intake is low and not a recognised major risk factor.
A symptom, not a risk factor, and most often from BPH.
Not a major risk factor in the notes.
Not established as a risk factor.

steps.x: A. Afro-Caribbean ethnicity. Prostate cancer risk: Afro-Caribbean ethnicity, BRCA1/2.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man is referred to the family history clinic. His mother had ovarian cancer at 49 and his sister had breast cancer at 41. Both carried the same germline mutation, and testing shows he carries it too. He asks whether it changes his risk of prostate cancer.
questions.q: Which mutation is he most likely to carry?
questions.e: Familial breast and ovarian cancer points to BRCA1 or BRCA2, and both increase the risk of prostate cancer in male carriers.

steps.x: The question asks: Which mutation is he most likely to carry? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Breast and ovarian cancer in a family.

elim: Causes familial adenomatous polyposis.
Causes cystic fibrosis.
Causes haemochromatosis.
Causes von Hippel-Lindau syndrome.

steps.x: B. BRCA1. BRCA1 and BRCA2 both raise prostate cancer risk.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man has lost 7 kg over 4 months. Today he passed blood clots and then could not pass urine. A catheter drains blood-stained urine with clots. Digital rectal examination shows a hard, craggy, fixed prostate. Investigations show a PSA of 88 µg/L (<4).
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.e: Weight loss and clot retention with a hard, craggy prostate and a very high PSA indicate prostate cancer.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Constitutional symptoms, clot retention and a malignant-feeling gland.

elim: The gland would be smooth, and the PSA would not be this high.
A common cause of clot retention, but would not cause a hard, craggy prostate and a very high PSA.
Causes haematuria and a loin mass, not a craggy prostate.
Does not cause haematuria with weight loss and a craggy gland.

steps.x: C. Prostate cancer. Weight loss, clot retention and a craggy gland = prostate cancer.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with prostate cancer and known vertebral metastases has thoracic back pain worse on lying down for 2 weeks. For 2 days he has been unable to hold his urine and his legs feel numb. His temperature is 36.8°C. Power in both legs is 4/5 and there is reduced sensation below the umbilicus.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his urinary incontinence?
questions.e: Back pain, limb weakness, sensory loss and bladder dysfunction in a man with vertebral metastases is metastatic spinal cord compression.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of his urinary incontinence? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Bony metastases plus a sensory level and new sphincter loss.

elim: Would not explain leg weakness and a sensory level.
Ascending weakness with areflexia and no sensory level or back pain from metastases.
Would not explain leg weakness and a sensory level.
He is afebrile and has neurological signs.

steps.x: C. Metastatic spinal cord compression. Prostate cancer + back pain + weakness + bladder dysfunction = MSCC.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man with metastatic prostate cancer trips on a step and cannot weight bear. X-ray shows a transverse fracture of the left femoral shaft passing through a dense, white, sclerotic area of bone. He has had aching in the thigh for 2 months.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the fracture?
o: Pathological fracture through an osteoblastic metastasis
questions.e: Prostate cancer bone metastases are osteoblastic (sclerotic), unlike osteolytic breast cancer metastases, and cause bone pain and pathological fractures.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of the fracture? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: aching in the thigh for 2 months
steps.x: Low-energy fracture through dense bone after weeks of pain.

elim: Osteoporosis makes bone thin and lucent, not dense and sclerotic.
Myeloma lesions are punched-out and lucent.
Typical of breast or renal cancer, not the dense lesion here.
Causes thickened bone, but in a man with metastatic prostate cancer a sclerotic deposit is far more likely.

steps.x: E. Pathological fracture through an osteoblastic metastasis. Prostate mets = sclerotic; fracture through them = pathological.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with locally advanced prostate cancer and bone metastases was started on goserelin 3 days ago. He was not given any other drug. He now has worsening pelvic bone pain and has been unable to pass urine for 8 hours. A tender, distended bladder is palpable.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his urinary retention?
questions.e: Goserelin can cause a transient tumour flare with bone pain, bladder obstruction and, with bony metastases, spinal cord compression.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of his urinary retention? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
New bone pain and obstruction days after starting a GnRH agonist alone.

elim: Goserelin is not anticholinergic.
Does not explain the timing just after starting goserelin with new bone pain.
There is no haematuria.
Causes polyuria and confusion, not acute retention.

steps.x: E. Tumour flare from goserelin. GnRH agonist without anti-androgen cover = tumour flare.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with prostate cancer and multiple vertebral metastases started leuprorelin 5 days ago without any other new medicine. He has new leg weakness and has been incontinent of urine. His temperature is 36.9°C. Power in both legs is 3/5 with a sensory level at T12.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Cauda equina syndrome from a disc prolapse
Spinal cord compression from tumour flare
questions.e: GnRH agonists cause an initial testosterone surge before suppression; in a man with vertebral metastases this flare can cause spinal cord compression.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
New cord signs days after a GnRH agonist with bony metastases.

elim: Cauda equina causes lower motor neurone signs without a thoracolumbar sensory level; he has vertebral metastases and a recent GnRH agonist.
No sensory level and usually follows infection.
Causes confusion and constipation, not a sensory level.
Not a recognised effect.

steps.x: E. Spinal cord compression from tumour flare. Flare + bony mets = spinal cord compression risk.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man has lower back pain for 3 months that is worse at night. He has lost 5 kg. His temperature is 36.7°C. There is tenderness over L3. Neurological examination of the legs is normal. Digital rectal examination shows a hard, irregular prostate. Investigations show a PSA of 140 µg/L (<4).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his back pain?
questions.e: Night pain, weight loss, a hard prostate and a very high PSA indicate bone metastases from prostate cancer.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of his back pain? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Red-flag back pain with a malignant prostate.

elim: Does not wake him at night or cause weight loss.
Does not cause a hard prostate and a very high PSA.
Would not explain the prostate findings and PSA.
His neurological examination is normal.

steps.x: A. Bone metastases from prostate cancer. Back pain + high PSA = bone metastases.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has newly diagnosed Gleason 4 + 5 = 9 prostate adenocarcinoma. His PSA is 64 µg/L (<4). He has no symptoms other than mild back ache. His team arranges staging.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of distant spread?
questions.e: The most common site of prostate cancer spread is bone, with osteoblastic lesions, especially in the spine; staging uses CT and a bone scan.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely site of distant spread? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
High-grade disease with back ache.

elim: Less common than bone.
Uncommon in prostate cancer.
Occurs late and is less common than bone.
Less common than bone.

steps.x: B. Bone. Prostate cancer spreads to bone (osteoblastic).

questions.stem: A 70 year old man had brachytherapy for T2N0M0 prostate cancer 4 months ago. He now has painful diarrhoea with fresh blood, and a constant feeling of needing to open his bowels. His temperature is 36.8°C. Stool culture is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.e: Brachytherapy for prostate cancer risks proctitis: bloody diarrhoea, tenesmus and painful diarrhoea.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: constant feeling of needing to open his bowels
steps.x: Rectal symptoms after prostate radiotherapy.

elim: Stool culture is negative and there is no recent antibiotic use.
Less likely given the clear link to recent pelvic radiotherapy.
Cause painless bright red bleeding, not painful diarrhoea and tenesmus.
A new presentation at 70 is less likely than radiation injury after brachytherapy.

steps.x: D. Radiation proctitis. Prostate radiotherapy → proctitis.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man sees his GP with mild nocturia. Digital rectal examination shows a hard, irregular left lobe of the prostate. He has no back pain or weight loss. His temperature is 36.6°C and BP 134/80 mmHg. Urine dipstick is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Prescribe tamsulosin and review in 3 months
Urgent 2-week-wait urology referral with a PSA
questions.e: NICE: a hard, irregular prostate on DRE warrants an urgent suspected cancer (2-week-wait) referral, with PSA measured alongside; secondary care then arranges multiparametric MRI.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: hard, irregular left lobe of the prostate
steps.x: A malignant-feeling prostate in primary care.

elim: Treats BPH symptoms and delays a suspected cancer referral.
Delays referral for a malignant-feeling gland.
A suspicious DRE needs the urgent pathway.
Biopsy follows MRI in secondary care.

steps.x: E. Urgent 2-week-wait urology referral with a PSA. Abnormal DRE = 2WW referral + PSA, then mpMRI.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has a PSA of 8.6 µg/L (<4) confirmed on repeat. He is seen in the rapid-access prostate clinic and has a multiparametric MRI of the prostate. The radiologist uses a 5-point scale to report how likely a lesion is to be clinically significant cancer.
questions.q: Which scoring system is being used?
questions.e: Multiparametric MRI of the prostate is scored with PI-RADS from 1 (very low) to 5 (very high); PI-RADS 3 or more leads to biopsy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which scoring system is being used? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
A 1 to 5 MRI likelihood score.

elim: Used for breast imaging.
Grades biopsy histology, not MRI.
Scores LUTS severity.
Describes extent of spread, not lesion likelihood on MRI.

steps.x: D. PI-RADS. mpMRI is reported with PI-RADS; ≥3 means biopsy.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with a PI-RADS 4 lesion has a transperineal prostate biopsy. The pathologist reports that the most common pattern in the samples is grade 4, and the second most common is grade 3.
questions.q: Which is the most likely Gleason score and grade?
questions.e: The Gleason score adds the most common pattern (first) and the second pattern, each out of 5: 6 or less is low, 7 intermediate and 8 to 10 high grade; a dominant 4 is worse than a dominant 3.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely Gleason score and grade? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: most common pattern in the samples is grade 4
steps.x: Primary pattern first, then secondary, then the grade band.

elim: The most common pattern goes first, and 7 is intermediate, not high.
The first number must be the most common pattern, which is 4.
7 is intermediate; 8 to 10 is high.
The second pattern is 3, not 4.

steps.x: D. 4 + 3 = 7, intermediate grade. Gleason: most common pattern first; ≤6 low, 7 intermediate, 8 to 10 high.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man has newly diagnosed prostate cancer. Biopsy shows Gleason 4 + 4 = 8 and his PSA is 32 µg/L (<4). He has mild lower back ache. His treatment depends on whether the disease has spread.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to stage his disease?
questions.e: Prostate cancer is staged with CT and a bone scan, because bone (osteoblastic lesions) is the most common site of spread.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation to stage his disease? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
High-risk disease needing staging.

elim: Does not stage nodes or bone.
Brain metastases are uncommon.
Confirms grade, not spread.
The liver is not the main site of spread.

steps.x: B. CT and isotope bone scan. Staging = CT + bone scan.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with metastatic prostate cancer has 10 days of worsening mid-back pain and, since yesterday, difficulty climbing stairs. His legs feel heavy. Plain X-ray of the thoracic spine shows sclerotic lesions in T8 and T9. His temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: CT of the thoracic spine in 2 weeks
Urgent MRI of the whole spine
questions.e: Urgent MRI of the whole spine is the gold standard for suspected metastatic spinal cord compression; surgical decompression may be needed.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: sclerotic lesions in T8 and T9
steps.x: Possible cord compression in a man with spinal metastases.

elim: Too slow and less sensitive for cord compression.
Shows bone metastases but not whether the cord is compressed.
Not used for suspected cord compression.
Delays the diagnosis.

steps.x: E. Urgent MRI of the whole spine. Suspected MSCC = urgent whole-spine MRI.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man had a robot-assisted radical prostatectomy for Gleason 3 + 4 = 7 prostate cancer. His PSA fell to undetectable within 3 months (see item resources). He is well, with mild stress incontinence that is improving.

visual.title: PSA after prostatectomy
visual.caption: PSA falls to undetectable after the gland is removed.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate follow-up?
o: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis every 3 months
PSA every 6 to 12 months for 5 years
questions.e: After prostatectomy, PSA is monitored every 6 to 12 months for 5 years to detect recurrence.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate follow-up? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Surveillance after surgery.

elim: Not needed while PSA remains undetectable.
Not routine; PSA is the monitoring tool.
Recurrence is detected by a rising PSA.
The prostate has been removed.

steps.x: D. PSA every 6 to 12 months for 5 years. Post-prostatectomy: PSA every 6 to 12 months for 5 years.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man with an enlarged prostate is brought in unable to pass urine for 14 hours. He has suprapubic pain and a tender bladder. A catheter drains 1300 mL. His pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 150/88 mmHg. He has had reduced urine output for several days.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate blood test to perform next?
questions.e: Acute urinary retention from an enlarged prostate risks an obstructive AKI, so serum creatinine must be checked; PSA should not be measured now.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate blood test to perform next? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: unable to pass urine for 14 hours
steps.x: Obstruction with a large volume: think kidneys.

elim: Not the priority after relieving retention.
Would be falsely raised by retention and catheterisation.
Not relevant here.
Not relevant to retention.

steps.x: B. Serum creatinine. Acute retention: check creatinine; delay PSA.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has a routine PSA of 4.7 µg/L (<4). He has no urinary symptoms and digital rectal examination is normal. On questioning, he ran a half-marathon the day before the test and had sexual intercourse the same night. He has had no recent infection.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Repeat PSA after 48 hours without ejaculation or vigorous exercise
questions.e: PSA is normal below 4; ejaculation and vigorous exercise within 48 hours raise it, so it should be repeated after 48 hours of avoidance.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: ran a half-marathon the day before
steps.x: A borderline result with two causes of a false rise.

elim: No evidence of cancer yet.
The PSA may be falsely raised; repeat it properly first.
Too long; the issue is test preparation.
Only after an abnormal MRI.

steps.x: C. Repeat PSA after 48 hours without ejaculation or vigorous exercise. Avoid ejaculation and vigorous exercise 48 hours before PSA.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man had acute urinary retention yesterday and has a urethral catheter in situ. A PSA taken in the emergency department is 11 µg/L (<4). Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, symmetrical, enlarged prostate. He has no weight loss or bone pain.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step regarding his PSA?
o: Repeat PSA once recovered from the retention and catheterisation
questions.e: PSA rises with urinary retention and recent instrumentation, so a value taken now is unreliable and should be repeated later before deciding on further tests.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step regarding his PSA? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
A raised PSA taken at the worst possible time.

elim: Staging is not indicated without a diagnosis of cancer.
There is no diagnosis of cancer.
Premature; the PSA is likely falsely raised.
Not needed to interpret this PSA.

steps.x: B. Repeat PSA once recovered from the retention and catheterisation. Retention and instrumentation raise PSA: repeat it later.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man has a PSA of 5.8 µg/L (<4). MRI shows a small PI-RADS 3 lesion confined to the prostate. Biopsy shows Gleason 3 + 3 = 6 adenocarcinoma in two cores. He is fit and chooses active surveillance.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate description of what active surveillance involves?
o: Androgen deprivation therapy with yearly review
Regular PSA, repeat MRI and repeat biopsy
questions.e: Active surveillance for localised low-grade disease means regular PSA monitoring, imaging and repeat Gleason scoring, with radical treatment if it progresses.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate description of what active surveillance involves? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Low-grade localised disease being monitored with curative intent.

elim: ADT is for advanced disease.
Not part of active surveillance for low-risk disease.
Describes watchful waiting rather than active surveillance.
Radical treatment is deferred in active surveillance.

steps.x: E. Regular PSA, repeat MRI and repeat biopsy. Active surveillance = PSA, MRI, repeat biopsy.

questions.stem: An 81 year old man with moderate dementia, ischaemic heart disease and a life expectancy estimated at under 5 years has low-risk prostate cancer. Biopsy shows Gleason 3 + 3 = 6 and his PSA is 6 µg/L (<4). He has no symptoms and there is no spread.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Low-risk disease with a life expectancy under 10 years or significant comorbidities is managed by watchful waiting, treating only if symptoms develop.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: life expectancy estimated at under 5 years
steps.x: Low-risk cancer in a frail man.

elim: For advanced or metastatic disease.
Curative treatment unlikely to benefit him.
Major surgery with no likely survival benefit.
Too aggressive for low-risk disease in a frail man.

steps.x: E. Watchful waiting. Low risk + short life expectancy = watchful waiting.

questions.stem: A 58 year old fit man has Gleason 4 + 4 = 8 prostate cancer confined to the prostate. CT and bone scan show no spread. He is planned for a robot-assisted laparoscopic radical prostatectomy and asks about the main long-term risks.
questions.q: Which are the most likely long-term complications to counsel him about?
questions.e: Radical prostatectomy (RALP is favoured over open surgery for fewer complications) commonly causes urinary incontinence and erectile dysfunction.

steps.x: The question asks: Which are the most likely long-term complications to counsel him about? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Counselling for radical surgery.

elim: Side effects of androgen deprivation therapy.
Not related to prostatectomy.
Complications of radiotherapy.
A typical effect of TURP, not the main counselling point after radical surgery.

steps.x: E. Urinary incontinence and erectile dysfunction. Prostatectomy: incontinence and erectile dysfunction.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has prostate cancer staged as T2N0M0. Biopsy shows Gleason 3 + 4 = 7. He wants curative treatment but would prefer to avoid a major operation. He has no bowel disease.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Brachytherapy is indicated for T2N0M0 disease as an alternative to surgery, with a risk of proctitis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: prefer to avoid a major operation
steps.x: Curative intent without surgery.

elim: Not curative for localised disease.
A form of androgen deprivation for advanced disease.
Treats BPH symptoms and is not a cancer treatment.
Not curative; he wants treatment and is fit.

steps.x: C. Brachytherapy. T2N0M0 and no surgery wanted = brachytherapy.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has newly diagnosed prostate cancer with a PSA of 210 µg/L (<4). A bone scan shows multiple metastases in the spine and pelvis. He has bone pain but no neurological symptoms. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 78 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
questions.e: Advanced disease is treated with androgen deprivation therapy: GnRH agonists such as goserelin or leuprorelin, or anti-androgens such as bicalutamide.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate long-term management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: multiple metastases in the spine and pelvis
steps.x: Metastatic disease.

elim: For localised low-grade disease.
For localised T2N0M0 disease, not widespread metastases.
Not used for metastatic disease.
He has symptomatic metastatic disease that needs treatment.

steps.x: B. Androgen deprivation therapy. Advanced prostate cancer = ADT.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man has newly diagnosed prostate cancer with a PSA of 96 µg/L (<4). A bone scan shows vertebral deposits. His oncologist plans to start goserelin next week. He has mild back ache but no neurological symptoms, and his pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 140/82 mmHg. He asks whether anything should be started first.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate drug to start before goserelin?
questions.e: Goserelin causes a transient tumour flare, so an anti-androgen (flutamide or cyproterone acetate) is started first to block the testosterone surge.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate drug to start before goserelin? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Flare risk with spinal metastases.

elim: For established cord compression, not routine flare prevention.
A BPH treatment, not flare prevention.
Treats LUTS, not tumour flare.
Protects bone but does not prevent the testosterone surge.

steps.x: C. Flutamide. Before a GnRH agonist: flutamide or cyproterone acetate.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with metastatic prostate cancer has progressive leg weakness. Urgent MRI shows a single metastasis compressing the spinal cord at T10. He has been given dexamethasone 16 mg. He was fully active until a week ago and his cancer is otherwise controlled.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Oral morphine and review in 1 week
questions.e: Metastatic spinal cord compression is confirmed with urgent MRI, and in a fit patient with good prognosis surgical decompression may be required.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: compressing the spinal cord at T10
fully active until a week ago
steps.x: Confirmed cord compression in a fit man.

elim: Does not relieve compression.
Does not act quickly enough on cord compression.
Delay risks permanent paralysis.
The diagnosis is confirmed; treat now.

steps.x: E. Surgical decompression. MSCC: urgent MRI, then decompression if fit.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man has a PSA of 38 µg/L (<4) and a hard, irregular prostate on digital rectal examination. He has no urinary infection and has not had recent instrumentation. Biopsy shows adenocarcinoma with disorganised glands. He asks why a cancer makes this blood test rise.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the raised PSA?
o: Glandular disruption letting PSA from epithelial cells into the blood
questions.e: PSA is a serine protease made by prostatic epithelial cells; cancer disrupts the glands so more enters the blood.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation for the raised PSA? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
A high PSA with disrupted glands.

elim: PSA comes from prostatic epithelium, not bone.
PSA is not made in the liver.
Not the reason PSA is raised in cancer.
PSA is made by epithelial cells.

steps.x: B. Glandular disruption letting PSA from epithelial cells into the blood. PSA = serine protease from epithelium; leaks with glandular disruption.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has a PSA of 15 µg/L (<4) at a health check. He has no urinary symptoms at all. Biopsy shows Gleason 3 + 4 = 7 adenocarcinoma in the posterior gland. He asks why he never had trouble passing urine.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the absence of urinary symptoms?
o: Prostate cancer arises in the transition zone
The tumour arises in the peripheral zone away from the urethra
The tumour has spread to bone
questions.e: Prostate cancer arises in the peripheral zone, so it does not typically cause early obstructive symptoms or acute retention, unlike transition-zone BPH.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation for the absence of urinary symptoms? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
A posterior tumour without LUTS.

elim: It grows; the issue is where.
The transition zone is the site of BPH.
He has no obstruction to compensate for.
Spread would not explain the lack of urinary symptoms.

steps.x: D. The tumour arises in the peripheral zone away from the urethra. Peripheral zone cancer rarely obstructs early.

questions.stem: Two men have prostate biopsies. The first shows Gleason 3 + 3 = 6, with small, uniform, well-formed glands. The second shows Gleason 5 + 4 = 9, with sheets of cells and few recognisable glands. The second man has a much worse prognosis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason the Gleason score predicts prognosis?
o: It measures the number of cores involved
It reflects loss of normal glandular architecture
It reflects spread to lymph nodes
questions.e: Gleason grading reflects loss of normal glandular architecture; higher patterns are more disorganised and infiltrative, which correlates with worse prognosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely reason the Gleason score predicts prognosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Architecture is what differs.

elim: Gleason is histological, not biochemical.
It is based on pattern, not core count.
Size is part of the T stage, not Gleason.
Nodal spread is the N stage.

steps.x: D. It reflects loss of normal glandular architecture. Gleason = architecture; more disorganised = worse.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with metastatic prostate cancer has been on goserelin for 3 months. His testosterone is now at castrate levels, although it rose in the first week. His PSA has fallen from 120 to 8 µg/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which goserelin now suppresses testosterone?
o: Blockade of androgen receptors on tumour cells
questions.e: GnRH agonists first stimulate then downregulate pituitary GnRH receptors, so LH and testosterone fall after an initial surge.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism by which goserelin now suppresses testosterone? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
An initial rise followed by suppression.

elim: The mechanism of bicalutamide and flutamide.
Goserelin acts on the pituitary.
The mechanism of finasteride.
Not its mechanism.

steps.x: C. Downregulation of pituitary GnRH receptors. GnRH agonist: stimulates, then downregulates, the pituitary.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with metastatic prostate cancer starts androgen deprivation therapy. Over 6 months his bone pain eases, his PSA falls and repeat imaging shows the metastases have stopped growing. He asks why lowering testosterone controls the cancer.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Androgens are needed for osteoblast survival
Low testosterone activates cytotoxic T cells
Low testosterone reduces PSA production only
Prostate cancer growth depends on androgens
Testosterone is converted into oestrogen in tumour cells
questions.e: ADT works by exploiting the androgen dependence of prostate cancer growth.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
A tumour responding to hormone removal.

elim: The effect is on the tumour, not bone cells.
Not the mechanism of ADT.
The tumour itself shrinks, not just the marker.
Not the basis of ADT.

steps.x: D. Prostate cancer growth depends on androgens. ADT exploits androgen dependence.
